item.title: 'Misfortune creates empathy' - Mikel Landa finally finds redemption on toughest Vuelta a España stage
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: It's been five years since Mikel Landa last won a bike race, and 11 since he claimed his previous Grand Tour triumph in a stage of the Vuelta a España, but the Basque racer finally pulled off what had seemed to be Mission Impossible with a stunning solo victory on the 2026 Vuelta's toughest mountain stage.Visibly emotional as he crossed the line alone and with a more than sufficient 47-second advantage over second-placed Tobias Johannessen (Uno X-Mobility), Landa continued to choke up with emotion during the press conference that followed. The Soudal-QuickStep racer has had more than his fair share of crashes and injuries during his career, most recently in the Itzulia-Basque Country when he fractured his pelvis after being hit by a race organisation vehicle on a descent.That set him back weeks, if not months, and he came to the Vuelta a España saying he had never been so uncertain about whether he could race well; even earlier this week, he told one Spanish newspaper this had been the worst year of his career.That suddenly changed completely when he managed to make it into the break of the day after a long chase through the mountains of Granada and then managed to drop the last remnants of a move dominated by Uno-X riders at the foot of the last climb of the stage, the Collado del Alguacil.All that uncertainty melted away on the climb as Landa, one of the most popular racers in Spain, managed to keep Johannessen at a distance to clinch an enormous victory, just when it seemed least possible. Small wonder that the emotions came through so strongly, then, as Landa explained to the media why so many fans were pleased when he finally succeeded against all the odds"Misfortunes create a lot of empathy," Landa said. "It's harder to feel such a high degree of empathy for somebody when they succeed all the time, like Tadej Pogačar, say. I'm like a lot of people in life in general, who have a lot of bad moments and only a few very good ones.""I certainly had to fight for this victory a lot, because I had a lot of bad moments in the second week in particular, but I didn't want to go home without trying, and today I tried a lot harder."I'm generally a very optimistic person, I just needed a bit of help and I knew sooner or later it would come. I've had a lot of support throughout the year from my team" - which he will be leaving at the end of this season - "and I just kept on hoping."Landa said he had been very cross with himself, too, for failing to make it into the key break of stage 19, so he had pushed himself hard to bridge across from a chase group of 50 to the front group of 14 halfway through stage 20. It was a risky strategy, he said, and he tried to time his move so that he would be able to catch his breath after the second of the four major climbs of the day. Then after that, it was a question of staying close to the front and waiting to make his move."I was still doubting when I attacked about seven or eight kilometres from the top, and I thought that I wouldn't be able to go all the way to the line. But after that, the gap opened wider and wider, and I think all the energy I hadn't been able to use in the weeks beforehand, finally came through when it mattered the most," Landa said.Whilst the support from his team was critical - and the huge hug he received from sports director Tom Steels halfway through his press conference was testament to how much it mattered to Soudal-QuickStep on all levels, too - Landa said he had been able to dig so deep on the final climb precisely because as this was the last high mountains stage, he knew it was his last chance to try for it. At the same time, he said, thinking about getting a win to dedicate to his children also inspired him to keep trying."This win wasn't just about Watts and power, it was also about experience and knowing when to go for it," he explained. "But most of all it was about motivation, and I was feeling very motivated to try for it."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'Maybe it was a bit boring to watch' – Felix Gall refuses to crack despite onslaught of attacks from Richard Carapaz on Vuelta a España queen stage
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: After traversing a day of complete chaos and surviving what felt like 100 attacks from Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost), Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) should add a podium finish at the Vuelta a España to the one he already earned at the Giro d'Italia if he finishes stage 21 into Granada. Try, try, and try again, as he may, Gall always had the answer, and in the end, he actually managed to extend his lead over Carapaz and move away from race leader Enric Mas (Movistar) on the final, brutal climb, capping off 20 more excellent days of racing in 2026. "We maybe got caught a bit off guard with the crosswinds at the start. It was maybe a bit of a slap, a wake-up call, then Movistar slowed it down," said Gall, who was caught behind in one of the splits when racing exploded on an exposed, straight road with 175km to go. "We did think about going for the stage today, or trying to control it, but with losing Matthew [Riccitello], then just with five riders left, we said we'd sit in the wheels and see. And as expected, Richie [Carapaz] was making it pretty hard for me and then on the final climb, I just wanted to finish on a strong note here. For sure I'm happy; a super tough day."Someone will likely need to show Gall a replay of the stage when his legs and head are back at full strength, as he summed up his impressive display of defence – best shown at the summit of the first time up Puerto de el Purche, where Carapaz exploded things into life with just under 100 to go – as "boring."Having failed to get the gap he wanted and been foiled at every attempt by an undying Gall, who was more than a worthy opponent, Carapaz had no regrets about his tactics, set to finish the Vuelta in fourth after proving to be the master animator in these past few days. "[In the] final, I had nothing to lose and lots to win; the team did great, tried to race a different kind of race, not just waiting for the end, happy with how I did," said Carapaz to reporters at the line. "Especially the first two attacks, they really hurt," said Gall when asked about the swashbuckling Ecuadorian. "He's so explosive; he knows exactly when and how to do it. "Then maybe it was a bit boring to watch, but I had to just sit on his wheel all day, and I didn't want to close a gap on him again. You don't let that guy, such a strong rider, get up the road."Gall didn't read too much into finishing 17 seconds quicker than Mas up the final climb, reasoning that "He has a bit of a cushion he can work with, so maybe he didn't want to put himself into too much pain, but of course it's nice to finish like that," but he could take pride in that; if he is to make it safely to the line near the Alhambra tomorrow, that will almost finish his season off with two elite Grand Tour performances to his name. "First we have to finish tomorrow's stage, but I mean it's been a super good season so far; if I finish tomorrow," said Gall, with a hilly route potentially offering a final chance to come unstuck on Sunday. "The big goal was to fight for a podium in a Grand Tour, and I managed to do it in Giro, which went super well, and I'm really happy I was able to be in such good shape here again. Just very happy and I think good for my development."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'You can't win a Grand Tour without suffering' - as Vuelta a España victory beckons, Enric Mas reveals battle to overcome tough challenges
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: With just 24 hours left before he claims overall victory in the Vuelta a España and after coming through the last mountain stage without any major incidents, Enric Mas has revealed that while there were some tough moments en route to what will be the biggest triumph of his career, he knew how to handle them.On the hardest climbing stage of the entire Vuelta with nearly 5,000 metres of vertical climbing, the 31-year-old did not try to go for a second summit victory, instead opting to ride within himself and keep his closest rivals under control. His strategy proved a resounding success, as after an early phase before the climbs where crosswinds briefly threatened to implode his hold on GC, Mas did not experience any significant attacks.Richard Carapaz tried, without success, to go from distance with a long-range move 90 kilometres from the line, and even the EF Education-EasyPost rider, fourth overall, said afterwards he had only tried because he knew Mas did not consider him a threat.Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) did drop Mas on the final ascent to the Collado del Alguacil but only gained 17 seconds on the Spaniard. Rather than trouble Mas, Gall's primary goal was to drop Primoz Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), second overall, who finally crossed the line 38 seconds behind Mas at the line and 55 down on Gall. The Spaniard's superiority in the mountain stages in this year's Vuelta over Roglič, then, was once again clear, and with it, Mas' superiority in the overall classification. Barring absolute disaster on stage 21, Mas first Grand Tour victory in a race in which he already has four podium finishes is all but his for the taking."One day to go, like you said," Mas told reporters afterwards. "It's been a very emotive day, I have a lot of thoughts for my family, my team and everybody who supported me from the day I started riding a bike."I knew I was going very well even before the race started. I really didn't know if a podium was possible, but the training had gone very well since the Giro. So it all seemed to be going in a good way. I went for it on the day by day and it all went perfectly."Mas is now close to claiming Spain's first victory in the Vuelta since Alberto Contador in 2014, the first Grand Tour for his team since Carapaz in the Giro d'Italia in 2019 and the first of his career, at 31.However, after inheriting the red jersey when leading favourite Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) crashed out on stage 8, and Mas was running second overall, he said that if the pathway to victory had contained difficult moments, he'd known how to overcome them."You can't win a Grand Tour without suffering, there were very complicated moments where I was on the limit for a long time, but thanks to a long time and experience, I knew how to turn them round."At the same time, Mas adopted a strategy of not looking too far ahead to try and keep himself from getting overconfident, and it was a policy that paid off well."All the work I've done, I've done it for a moment like this," he said. "I've always dreamed about this. But I always tried to keep to a routine, I almost banned my soigneur from talking to me about what lay ahead, I even stopped him from making jokes about it. And," he said with a smile, "we've still got a day to go now."The final test over the four major climbs around Granada on stage 20 was one he passed more than comfortably, despite, as he said, the race being "a bit out of control in the first part," when echelons formed in the crosswinds.Once that moment had passed, "today I enjoyed every kilometre, I was counting them down during the race because I felt strong. I knew I was on a good day." Sunday's short, punchy stage could still hold a few surprises, and there are even some rumours that the very technical nature of the final, non-classified climb through the streets of Granada might see the GC times suspended before the last lap. But nearly two weeks after he inherited the red jersey from Pogačar, then proved to be more than up to the task of defending it successfully, Mas is almost there.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Winners and losers from Spanish GP F1 qualifying at the Madring
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: Just 0.011s separate first and second in the first-ever Formula 1 qualifying session at the Madring, and the first four slots on the Spanish Grand Prix grid will be occupied by drivers from four different teams too.But considering all the fears of a Sunday procession, is this the end of the action?And if it is, who's maximised their opportunity, and who's been found wanting?Loser: Oscar Piastri (7th)Eighth in Q1, ninth in Q2...Piastri was well off the pace throughout qualifying.He had to abort his first flying lap of Q1 and, from then on, it was a "messy" session by his reckoning.He even called it a "pretty crap" go in Q3, as he laboured to seventh."That's how it goes sometimes unfortunately," he said. "It's been a bit of a better weekend, like Monza, in that I at least am...happier with what the car's doing, and today was simply just one of those sessions."More painful will be the fact that it's expected to be hard to overtake here. And even more painful will be the fact that team-mate Lando Norris took a stunning pole position - so the pace was definitely there.Piastri's middling run continues. Winner: Lando Norris (1st)A winner not just because of the end result, but because of the manner in which it arrived - pretty much out of nowhere.The earlier stages of qualifying suggested this would be a fight between Mercedes and Ferrari, with Max Verstappen's Red Bull maybe interloping.Norris was fifth in Q1 but only seventh in Q2, and when Kimi Antonelli stuck his Mercedes on provisional pole with the first 1m31s lap of the weekend, having been narrowly usurped by Lewis Hamilton in the first Q3 runs, it looked at though the session was going to form.But then came Norris, with a full-send, ultra-committed lap in his McLaren.The last corner was untidy - team principal Andrea Stella reckoned Norris lost three tenths there - but the rest of it Stella called "a masterpiece", and what Norris reckoned was probably the best qualifying lap of his entire career was enough to snatch pole from Antonelli by a hundredth of a second.Not totally clean from the world champion, but certainly brilliant. Loser: George Russell (6th)Gap to Antonelli in pace: 0.314s (not great)Gap to Antonelli in positions: four (also not great)Russell seemed shake off his brush with the wall in Q1, a session he ended up topping, pretty easily and said he felt in a good place afterwards - claiming he was "about three tenths up" on his previous best midway round his final Q3 lap."Tried pushing hard in Turn 11, the tyres couldn't take it and then lost all the laptime thereafter," said Russell, who added it has been "really challenging" to judge how hard to lean on the tyres.Salvaging a time loss in that three-tenth ballpark obviously would've made a difference to his grid position. But after a promising start to the weekend, qualifying was another example of Russell being a step behind at Mercedes - and barely being able to grasp at any title hopes right now. Winner: Lewis Hamilton (4th)Hamilton outqualified Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc by just 0.006s and did well to take a place on the second row after crashing and losing time in FP3.The seven-time champion delivered a terse post-qualifying summary as he recalled a "pretty straightforward" session and praised "good execution" from the team."I'm going to have fun, that's all I can say, I’m going to have real fun, I'm not going to put too much pressure on it," he said.Leclerc, who is using an older-spec Ferrari engine after his Monza crash, said he lost time through sector one in particular."I think most of the people put a new power unit or a newer-spec [in for qualifying], and I kind of had the same spec - and that's on me obviously for last week - so maybe I didn't do the step forward that the others did on that side," he said."But having said that I think the lap was quite clean. I've had a few moments here and there, which I maybe lost a little bit and when I see how close it is, it's frustrating but at the same time I feel like if you ask any drivers on the grid today, everybody probably can find something on the lap."After their clash at the start of the Italian GP, the spotlight will again be on the Ferrari drivers at the start of this race in Madrid. Loser: Ollie Bearman (21st)That crash ruled him out of qualifying and put him a provisional 21st on the grid.Painful - as Haas team-mate Esteban Ocon was up in 13th."It's a shame to be standing here right now," said Bearman as he stood watching on from the sidelines in qualifying. "The car was quick. Yesterday was a tough day but we made some changes overnight and the car was feeling really good in FP3."Unfortunately I got caught out in Turn 10 on that final lap."He said worn tyres and a gust of wind contributed to his mistake.Sunday could be Bearman's ninth-straight grand prix without points, and Haas's eighth, as Audi continues to chip away at its advantage in the fight for seventh in the constructors' championship. Winner: Max Verstappen (3rd)Another typical Red Bull turnaround from Friday, when technical director Pierre Wache indicated his team needed to work on set-up, mechanical grip, ride quality and energy deployment in order to get Verstappen into a better position.The four-time champion was knocking on the door in FP3, just under four tenths off the pace, and come qualifying he was right in the mix: 0.170s off the pace in Q1 (where team-mate Liam Lawson lapped within a tenth of Russell's Mercedes) then fastest of all in Q2.Verstappen was one of only three drivers to lap below 1m32s in Q3, enough to place him third on the grid and ahead of both Ferraris, a Mercedes and a McLaren, while Lawson faded to eighth.Verstappen credited the car for finally doing what he wanted it to in the corners, but it's hard to escape the feeling there was also a bit of Max magic in play to make the difference in the end. Loser: Pierre Gasly (14th)Baffled and bemused. That's how best to describe Gasly at the end of qualifying."Something doesn't add up," he lamented after qualifying 14th, an uncharacteristic seven tenths off Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto in Q2.He suggested he'd never felt such a switch from where the car had been - on Friday, it had left him confident of making the top 10 - to where it ended up. "All my traction, I'm laying rubber every corner, sideways in all the high speed," said Gasly, who tentatively concurred when The Race asked whether this might be a deeper, set-up related issue.Asked if he expected chaos or a procession in tomorrow's race, Gasly was in no mind to look ahead. "At the moment I just want to get back in the office and get the answers I need." Winner: Franco Colapinto (9th)One place worse off on the grid compared to last weekend, as Colapinto noted, but there were plenty of reasons to be happier with this performance than Q3 at Monza.Having gathered up a lairy moment at La Monumental on his first Q2 effort, Colapinto strung together a lap he called "amazing" that he was rightly proud of to progress to Q3.He felt this was a track more likely to be suited to Alpine's current midfield rivals Audi and Racing Bulls, an assessment that seems to have been supported by the general trend of the weekend so far - so the Alpine had little right leading the midfield, really.That it did owed everything to Colapinto replicating (actually improving) the laptime in Q3 - a potentially significant result on a weekend where the usually dependable Gasly has looked slightly off-colour. Loser: Aston Martin (18th & 21st)The Madring might be a temporary, street-style circuit, but it's still plenty fast enough and demanding enough on the power units to expose Honda.Fernando Alonso had a mighty good go at escaping Q1, but he needed another 81 thousandths of a second to leapfrog the two Williamses - cars Aston Martin has recently been spooking with its impressive rate of chassis improvement.Alonso felt he was losing "probably more than one second" because of the Honda engine.At least he managed to participate in the session, though, unlike team-mate Lance Stroll, who was parked by problems with his fresh engine's water pressure.Cadillac might be firmly in the rear view mirror now, but there's still clearly a massively long road to travel for Aston Martin to become even remotely as competitive as it wants to be and should be.

item.title: F1 2026 Spanish GP starting grid after two penalties
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: Lando Norris claimed pole position for the first Spanish Grand Prix to be held on Formula 1's new Madring circuit in Madrid, ahead of F1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli.Antonelli won't need to blast from the back to the front like he did last time out at Monza, though that may be difficult anyway given the nature of this new temporary circuit and how hard it looks to overtake on.Most drivers behaved themselves and there were no red flags in qualifying, despite fears this track would lead to frequent crashes.But there were a couple of grid penalties to account for: Carlos Sainz drops three places for impeding Valtteri Bottas in Q1, while Lance Stroll has a 40-place (!) penalty for taking a completely new Honda power unit that promptly sprung a water leak before he could set a time.Provisional Spanish GP starting grid1 Lando Norris (McLaren)2 Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes)3 Max Verstappen (Red Bull)4 Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)5 Charles Leclerc (Ferrari)6 George Russell (Mercedes)7 Oscar Piastri (McLaren)8 Liam Lawson (Red Bull)9 Franco Colapinto (Alpine)10 Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls)11 Nico Hulkenberg (Audi)12 Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi)14 Pierre Gasly (Alpine)15 Yuki Tsunoda (Racing Bulls)16 Alex Albon (Williams)17 Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)18 Sergio Perez (Cadillac)19 Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac)20 Carlos Sainz (Williams)22 Lance Stroll (Aston Martin)

item.title: New York Yankees vs. New York Mets: Gerrit Cole vs. Zac Thornton
item.author: Joshua Diemert
item.content:encoded: It’s been an emotional couple of days for the Yankees, with the storybook return of Anthony Volpe on Thursday almost immediately balanced by the weight of yesterday’s 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. If nothing else, the Yankees won both those games, and stand a good Gerrit Cole start away from likely taking another game, and another series, this afternoon taking on the Mets.Cole really has one job today — do not give up four home runs. One of the strangest starts you’ll ever see came last weekend in San Diego, where the veteran righty did just that against the Padres, and while they were all solo shots (with a back-to-back-to-back to begin the game), that fateful fourth allowed in the seventh made an ultimately-doomed comeback attempt impossible. Cole’s walk rate is Mars-class, and part of that tradeoff is often pitches in-zone that can be driven with authority, but he’s got to turn those fly balls into outs rather than free handouts to fans. If he does that today, I’m comfortable every time he takes the mound.Zac Thornton counters for the Mets, a player I’m unfamilar with overall but having quite a solid rookie turn in MLB. A 3.53 ERA is undercut but a FIP almost a full run higher, largely driven by the 2023 fifth-rounder’s low strikeout rate and a high HR rate that xFIP at least believes will be cut down a bit. The Yankee offense is looking a little more professional in recent days, but we’ve also seen how seemingly unknown lefties can torment them in 2026.Aaron Judge gets a half day off today, as he’ll DH facing the southpaw. This opens right field up for Heliot Ramos and his adventures on defense, while Paul Goldschmidt and Amed Rosario man the corners of the infield. Austin Wells has the catching duties even after playing in last night’s game.: Yankee Stadium — The Bronx, NY: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 (NYY), Audacy Mets Radio WHSQ 880AM, Audacy App 92.3 HD2 (NYM): Gotham Sports App, MLB.tv (out-of-market only)

item.title: Winners and losers from MotoGP’s Misano sprint
item.author: Eden Hannigan
item.content:encoded: Marc Marquez ran riot in the Misano MotoGP sprint - and he was the only rider who could really be particularly elated with how his San Marino Grand Prix Saturday has panned out.Here are our winners and losers from the 13-lap dress rehearsal race.Winner: Marc Marquez (1st)Marquez had looked all through the weekend as the only rider with a real shot of stopping Bezzecchi - but it was still a surprise in the end, both that he succeeded and how easy he made it look. After the sprint, he said that he thought a P2-P3 finish was on the cards with the soft rear. But with the medium, which he chose, "I was able to finish second-third... or victory!"The difference-maker was the extra margin the medium granted him, seemingly in terms of the rear pushing the front, and he exploited it very well - blasting past Bezzecchi at the start and then breaking his counter-charge with a lap 11 1m30.7s scorcher. As long as Sunday's result is any kind of decent points haul, this weekend is a success.Loser: Fabio Quartararo (21st)Before going in too hard on Quartararo, it is important to point out - he is the only Yamaha rider who looks like doing anything of note this weekend, and he is clearly trying.A crash is a crash, and it looked very clumsy, Quartararo trying to outfox Moreira but getting caught out under braking by what he described as "zero" rear support and running out of margin. But also a bit of a chapeau. There were a total of 11 sub-1m32s laps by Yamaha riders in this race - 10 of those were Quartararo after the crash, and the other one was Quartararo before the crash. The pace is there.Loser: Pecco Bagnaia (13th)“Honestly [it’s] difficult to speak about feeling when I don’t have any” was how Bagnaia opened his post-race debrief. We didn’t need him to tell us that though - the lack of feeling and control meant it was yet another fruitless sprint for the Ducati rider. Given Misano is a track Bagnaia has done countless laps around in the past, he could have been forgiven for expecting a slightly different outcome from this weekend. Instead, it looks to be more of the same as he’s running out of things to try to escape his troubles aboard the GP26. “Really frustrated but also humiliated” was how Bagnaia summed up how his struggles have made him feel. A performance like this in front of a home crowd can’t have helped his overall confidence.Winner: Jorge Martin (3rd)Martin lost points to both of his main title rivals at the conclusion of the 13 laps - but it looked on Friday like he would be losing a lot more than this, which is effectively bare minimum. He was very close to an unwanted Q1 ticket yesterday, but corrected some things on the bike and in his riding - though remained outmatched in qualifying trim."I cannot ride with the soft [rear]," Martin lamented. "That's why I am suffering in time attack. I feel it's pushing [the front] and everything gets so aggressive, and really difficult to manage the bike."Hence the choice of the medium for the sprint - and it clearly worked, enabling him to pick off Fermin Aldeguer and Fabio Di Giannantonio en route to a comfortable podium, even if the front was "cooked" by the laps behind the latter.Loser: Franco Morbidelli (12th)A rare opportunity for a genuinely good weekend in what has been a profoundly forlorn season is being squandered here for Morbidelli, who does genuinely look pretty decent on pure pace.But with a needless long lap penalty for impeding - imagine a long sigh in the middle of this sentence - meaning his Sunday is already compromised by default, perhaps the sprint was the big chance. Instead, he looked a bit timid over the first few corners, so got roughed up by Diogo Moreira and spent the rest of the race looking for a way back - which he never did find.Loser: Raul Fernandez/Trackhouse (7th)If Fernandez's assessment is accurate, this is much more of a Trackhouse entry than a Fernandez entry - as he says his Q2 was hamstrung by a "problem on both bikes", which meant he was three tenths slower than he had been in Q1. It had a huge knock-on on his grid position and meant his race prospects proved extremely limited as, after barging past Aldeguer, he got stuck behind Acosta and couldn't get the front tyre in a good enough state to give the KTM man anything to worry about.The Aprilia is clearly better than seventh place here, but on Trackhouse's side the reliability could certainly be improved.

item.title: Anthropic CEO says it’s time to pump the brakes on AI
item.author: Terrence O’Brien
item.content:encoded: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says the time has come to slow down AI development and will give third-party evaluators like METR access to its models to help ensure its "adherence to safety practices and commitments." In a winding essay, Amodei proposed a three-step plan to "pace the frontier" - jargon that simply means to slow the pace of training and development to give companies time to build safeguards and regulators to evaluate models.Amodei says that giving external evaluators wide-ranging access is just the first step, and one it is taking now unilaterally. Step two would involve the industry coming together as a whole, likely with gove …

item.title: Brent Headrick is chugging along in uncharted territory
item.author: Kento Mizuno
item.content:encoded: Though the Yankees have endured their fair share of misfortune this year – injuries to several key players come to mind – they’ve also enjoyed some positive surprises. Spencer Jones might be a viable big leaguer! Paul Goldschmidt wasn’t completely toast! Paul Blackburn’s running a sub-2.00 ERA! However, there’s one important development that I feel has flown under the radar at least a little bit, and that is Brent Headrick’s emergence as an elite reliever. Those of you following this team closely should need no reminder of how good Headrick has been, but his performance to date stands out even when compared to the rest of the league. Here’s how Brent’s key stats rank among all qualified MLB relievers.fWAR: (2.2, tied with Trevor Megill)IP: (73.1)ERA: (1.96)ERA-: (47)FIP: (2.31)FIP-: (54, tied with Mason Montgomery)K-BB%: (22.0%)No matter how you slice it, Headrick’s 2026 performance to date has been nothing short of elite. However, I want to call attention to one stat in particular: his innings count. With about three weeks still remaining in the season, Headrick has already thrown 73.1 innings, the most he’s ever thrown in the majors by far. In fact, even when accounting for his minor league stats, his 2026 workload still stands out.Headrick did throw 108.1 innings across High-A and Double-A in 2022, followed by 100.2 innings across Triple-A and the majors in 2023. However, that was when he was primarily a swingman, with 35 out of his 58 appearances during that time being starts. Having since moved to a full-time relief role, Headrick accumulated just 69.1 innings ]over 2024 and 2025 across the minors and the majors. In other words, 2026 Headrick has already thrown more innings than his previous two years combined. If I were him, I’d be asking for a hefty raise in the offseason if I wasn’t pre-arb.With any pitcher — and perhaps doubly so for relievers, who are as a group inherently fickle — a marked increase in workload comes with two red flags: heightened injury risk, and potential decline in performance. I can’t speak on the former, as I’m not a medical professional. However, I can provide some assurance regarding the latter, as despite being worked harder than ever before, Headrick isn’t showing many signs of slowing down.Yes, it’s true that Headrick’s ERA has risen a bit recently. From the start of the season through July, he posted a 1.30 ERA in 55.1 innings. Since then? A 4.00 mark across 18 innings. However, a look at Headrick’s underlying numbers suggests that this has more to do with bad luck than his workload catching up to him.If Headrick was truly gassed, we’d expect that to show in several areas of his FanGraphs page. For example, if his stuff was diminished, we’d expect his strikeout rate to decrease and his walk rate to increase. But looking at his splits pre- and post-August, the opposite has happened. Headrick’s actually fanning batters at a higher rate since August 1st (32.2%) than before (29.4%), while his walk rate since (7.4%) is also slightly lower than before (7.8%), even including last night’s two-walk outing. If there has been a decline in Headrick’s stuff, it sure isn’t showing up here.Of course, it might be that Headrick is allowing harder contact as he runs on fumes. However, the data doesn’t really support this hypothesis either. His hard contact rate was 26.4 percent from March-July, and from the start of August onward that has risen all the way to … 26.5 percent. His batted-ball mix is basically the same, too—he’s generated grounders and fly balls at roughly the same rates. The only difference is that recently more of his fly balls allowed have been leaving the park. His HR/FB rate was a miniscule 3.4 percent prior to August, but since then that’s jumped up to 10.5 percent. However, HR/FB has proven to be a fickle statistic, and very few pitchers have shown the ability to consistently suppress it. Given the fact that a 10.5 percent HR/FB is still below league average, I’m comfortable saying that this shouldn’t be cause for alarm.The most likely culprit for Headrick’s heightened ERA seems to be worse luck on batted balls. Here’s his 15-game rolling BABIP, through the beginning of play yesterday: If we superimpose his 15-game rolling ERA- trends on this graph, we can see how closely the two trends coincide:And if we compare that to his FIP- trends, we can see how Headrick’s core skills have remained consistent despite fluctuations in his surface stats:So, in my humble opinion, the fact that Headrick’s ERA has risen a bit of late shouldn’t scare you.At Headrick’s core, he’s still the shutdown reliever he was earlier in the year; he’s just run into a patch of bad luck. Of course, this doesn’t preclude the possibility to Headrick’s workload catching up to him eventually, and we’d be remiss if we didn’t note that his average fastball velocity in September (93.2 mph) is lower than any previous month (below May’s 93.9 mph). It’s not an enormous dip and it’s possible that the adrenaline of the postseason could boost it back up in certain outings.Nonetheless, Aaron Boone and Matt Blake should of course be monitoring his health closely; going into the playoffs without a fully functioning Headrick would be less than ideal, to say the least. As of now however, Headrick seems to be just fine, and that’s good news for the Yankees as they enter the most crucial part of the season.

item.title: Vuelta a España Stage 20: Landa Rescues Terrible Season, Mas Set for Overall Win

item.title: Vuelta a España: Enric Mas passes arduous final mountain test to keep red as Mikel Landa soars to stage 20 breakaway victory atop Collado del Alguacil
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Enric Mas (Movistar) put the finishing touches on a certain Vuelta a España victory atop the steep slopes of the Collado de Alguacil, the Spaniard surviving a day of long-range GC action to hold onto the red jersey after five hours of racing.There was double celebration for Spain on the penultimate stage of the Vuelta as Mikel Landa (Soudal-QuickStep) proved the strongest from the day's breakaway, leaving behind Tobias Halland Johannessen (Uno-X Mobility) and Ramses Debruyne (Alpecin-Premier Tech) to solo up the final climb and take his first win in five years.The win is the 17th of Landa's career and the first since the 2021 Vuelta a Burgos. It's almost certain to be his last for Soudal-QuickStep, with the Basque rider set to 'go home' with a move to Euskaltel-Euskadi next season.Behind the breakaway battle, the GC battle raged over four of the 186.8km stage's five major climbs, with Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) attacking time and again in search of a podium spot and Sepp Kuss (Visma-Lease a Bike) launching a long-range move to move well into the GC top 10.Mas raced into the final climb of the stage and its double-digit gradients untroubled, however, with his nearest rival Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) unable to make a decisive move to overcome that 1:37 GC gap.In the end, it was Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) who made the first major attack, taking Mas with him as he aimed at Roglič's second place. He proved the strongest of the GC men on the final climb, racing to the line 6:37 down on Landa and 55 seconds up on Roglič.Mas crossed the line at 6:54, having shed some time to Gall but with his red jersey intact and heading into Sunday's closing stage with an extended 2:15 advantage over second-placed Roglič and his Vuelta win all but confirmed.Kuss' ride to eighth on the stage, meanwhile, delivered him to fifth overall, jumping up six places in the GC to 8:45 behind Mas, 43 seconds up on Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos).The penultimate stage of the Vuelta a España posed the last big challenge of the race, taking the peloton on a 186.8km run through the mountains with five classified climbs and a summit finish atop the Collado del Alguacil on the menu.The early third-category climb of the Puerto de Blacares (7.7km at 3.7%) led to two ascents of the first-category climb, the Puerto de El Purche (8.2km at 8.1%), before another first-category climb of the Puerto de El Duque (7.4km at 8.3%) and then the closer, the HC-rated Collado del Alguacil (8km at 9.8%).Attacks flew from the start of the stage, with Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Ivo Oliveira (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) among the first riders to jump clear at the front. Winds blowing early in the stage only complicated matters, provoking a split in the peloton.Race leader Enric Mas was among the notable names caught out in the split, but the Spaniard quickly sent his Movistar group to the front to rectify the situation and get back to the front.Moves continued to go clear at the front, meanwhile, with a large group breaking free after 30km of racing. Joining Van Aert and Oliveira were six Uno-X Mobility riders in Tobias Halland Johanessen, Simon Dalby, Andreas Kron, Magnus Cort, Andreas Leknessund, and Rasmus Tiller. Also in the move were Bryan Coquard, Louis Rouland (Cofidis), Finn Fisher-Black, Gianni Vermeersch (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Oscar Chamberlain (Decathlon CMA CGM), and Pau Miquel (Bahrain Victorious).Movistar continued to lead the way behind as another group split off the front in pursuit of the breakaway. The larger group got away after 50km of racing, and some 50 riders made the move.Movistar placed three men in the move with Iván Romeo, Raúl García Pierna and Pablo Castrillo, while a host of other notable names made the group. Mountain classification leader Santiago Buitrago (Bahrain Victorious), Kevin Vermaerke (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike), Eddie Dunbar (Pinarello-Q36.5), Jack Haig (Netcompany Ineos), Thibau Nys (Lidl-Trek), Ramses Debruyne (Alpecin-Premier Tech), Valentin Paret-Peintre, Mikel Landa (Soudal-QuickStep), Marco Brenner (Tudor), Lorenzo Fortunato (XDS-Astana), Jarno Widar (Lotto-Intermarché), Luke Tuckwell (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Urko Berrade (Kern Pharma), and Jan Hirt (NSN) were all in there.After 80km of racing, as the race approached the first ascent of the Puerto de El Purche, the peloton lay nine minutes adrift of the leaders, while the 50-man chase group were 3:20 down. With the breakaway groups settled out front, there wasn't much longer to wait until the first big move of the day came from behind as Sepp Kuss (Visma-Lease a Bike) launched a move 97km from the line, his attack followed by Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) 2km later.Decathlon CMA CGM, without Matthew Riccitello who crashed out earlier in the day, worked in the chase behind with Felix Gall taking a leading role. Gall – with Mas and Roglič on his wheel and Onley trailing close behind – caught Carapaz and Kuss going over the top, the peloton already shattered with half the stage to go.As riders, including Brennan, Vincenzo Albanese (EF Education-EasyPost), and Sander De Pestel (Decathlon CMA CGM), dropped back from the break to help their GC leaders, Onley was only shedding time, racing up the second ascent of the Puerto de El Purche at three minutes down.Up front, still eight minutes clear, Uno-X Mobility continued to lead the front group as green jersey Van Aert – 38 mountain points down on Buitrago – grabbed the maximum of 20 over the two climbs of El Purche.Back in the GC group, Kuss attacked once more and went over the top of the climb with a minute lead as the GC group continued to sweep up riders dropped from the big breakaway group, including García Pierna to assist Mas.The leaders raced through the intermediate sprint and onto the Puerto de El Duque with an 8:30 advantage over the red jersey group. It wasn't long before the attacks came at the front, with Johannessen jumping, accompanied by Landa and Debruyne, who had earlier bridged across from the large chase group.As the GC men approached the top of the climb, the cat-and-mouse games broke out, with the pace nearing trackstand territory at one point as the gap to the leaders ballooned out to 9:30. Carapaz, who made several moves on the way up, couldn't dislodge any of his companions. Meanwhile, Romeo dropped back before the summit to help Mas.There was little change in the situation on the road to the final climb, with the leaders starting the ascent nine minutes up on the GC contenders and their satellite helper teammates. Kuss, meanwhile, was five minutes up on Mas and co, racing from 11th overall into the virtual top five with Van Aert and Jørgen Nordhagen working for him.At 7km from the line, Landa made his move, dropping Debruyne and putting Johannessen in trouble. James Shaw worked for Carapaz at the head of the GC group, meanwhile, with the big moves yet to come.Pablo Castrillo, the last Movistar man to drop back from the break, led the GC group up the climb, his pace putting off others from jumping. Once he was done, however, Gall made a move. The Austrian took Mas with him, but Roglič and Carapaz couldn't go with them. Gall quickly put 30 seconds into Roglič as he sought out second overall on the final mountain of the Vuelta.It was Landa who reached the top first, celebrating victory from the breakaway after a brutal day in the breakaway to cross the line 49 seconds up on Johannessen as Debruyne trailed home in third place.As the Basque rider celebrated his win, Gall left Mas behind heading into the final 2km in an attempt to put the 1:24 he needed between him and Roglič. He put up a big fight, but wouldn't overhaul the Slovenian, instead consolidating his third place overall at the line.Mas, meanwhile, rolled home with no threats to his overall lead and with his red jersey safe once more ahead of the final stage in Granada.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. You'll get comprehensive race coverage of La Vuelta a España, subscriber-exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. item.author: Michelle Goldberg
item.content:encoded: Silicon Valley’s strange new theology.

item.title: Why Marquez opted for an offset strategy in MotoGP San Marino GP sprint
item.content:encoded: Marc Marquez revealed he made a last-minute decision to switch to Michelin’s medium rear tyre, which ultimately proved decisive in his victory in MotoGP's San Marino Grand Prix sprint.While 15 of the 21 riders opted for the soft compound on Saturday, citing low tyre degradation at Misano, Marquez was among the minority to race with the medium in the sprint.This strategy put him at odds ...Keep reading

item.title: ‘We must slow the pace’: CEO of Anthropic calls for an AI slowdown
item.author: Edward Helmore
item.content:encoded: In a social media post, Dario Amodei proposed a plan including third-party evaluations of AI systemsThe CEO of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic issued a new appeal on Saturday for the AI industry to “slow down” and offered a three-part plan for doing so, saying that his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps.In a post on social media, Dario Amodei shared a link to an essay titled We Must Pace the Frontier in which he lays out how Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”.Continue reading...

item.title: Trump Says He’d Love to See a ‘United’ Ireland During Visit
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump says he would like to see Ireland “unified,” a remark that puts him at odds with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham who recently said the issue is off the table. Olivia Fletcher reports. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Pointed! Bloomberg's Weekly News Quiz For Risk-Takers
item.content:encoded: Pointed offers a strategic twist to the news quiz format, testing not just players’ knowledge of the news but also their confidence in their answers. Join Bloomberg's Lisa Mateo, Christina Ruffini, and Jeff Mason as they play and check out the quiz for yourself at Bloomberg.com (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Saudi Arabia shuts down key oil pipeline, blaming drones from Iraq
item.author: Oliver Holmes and agencies
item.content:encoded: Riyadh has increased use of East-West pipeline since start of war on Iran to bypass closure of strait of HormuzSaudi Arabia has shut down a critical oil pipeline, accusing militants in Iraq of launching drone attacks on the export route being used to bypass the lockdown of the strait of Hormuz.The world’s largest ⁠crude oil exporter has increased its use of the 745-mile (1,200km) pipeline running across the Arabian peninsula, which links Abqaiq, near the Gulf, to the port of Yanbu, on the Red Sea, since the US-Israeli war against Iran began.Continue reading...

item.title: Trump’s Foes Find Common Ground at Modi’s New Delhi Summit
item.author: Dan Strumpf, Sudhi Ranjan Sen, Ilya Arkhipov and Josh Xiao
item.content:encoded: Leaders of emerging powers including Russia and Iran projected a united front at a weekend summit in New Delhi, with a joint statement that targeted a US-launched war in the Middle East, Washington’s tariff campaign and its sanctions policy.

item.title: Iran War Revives Lessons of Iraq for Fukuyama
item.content:encoded: Joining David Gura on Bloomberg This Weekend, Stanford Spogli Institute for International Studies Senior Fellow Francis Fukuyama says the Iran war risks repeating lessons from Iraq and Afghanistan, arguing that military power alone is unlikely to produce lasting political change. In discussing his new memoir, In the Realm of the Last Man, he also warns that the rapid advance of AI could outpace governments' ability to regulate it and challenge the role that work plays in giving people purpose. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: How Trump Is Wielding Power to Stifle Speech
item.author: Jim Rutenberg and Maggie Haberman
item.content:encoded: President Trump has harnessed agencies across the government to curtail press freedoms, a sweeping campaign that free speech advocates say will have lasting effects.

item.title: Bezzecchi defends start after Marquez passes him again in Misano sprint
LG responds to TV spying allegations
item.author: Terrence O’Brien
item.content:encoded: Earlier this week, Gamers Nexus, Level1Techs, and independent security researchers detailed some alarming findings about how LG's TVs are logging and uploading data on its users. Now the company is pushing back against those allegations, saying that "Some recent media coverage may have contributed to misconceptions about how LG smart TVs work."LG released a statement in which it claims that its "TVs do not continuously record or transmit users' conversations," and that wake-word detection is all processed locally. However, the word "continuously" is doing a lot of heavy lifting here as Gamers Nexus demonstrated an LG TV keeping extensive l …

item.title: Norris snatches first Madring Spanish GP pole from Antonelli
item.author: Samarth Kanal
item.content:encoded: Lando Norris snatched pole position for the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix from Formula 1 points leader Kimi Antonelli by just 0.011s in a breathless finale to qualifying at the Madring.With Lewis Hamilton on provisional pole for Ferrari (1m32.079s) ahead of the Mercedes drivers after the first Q3 runs, Red Bull's Max Verstappen and the McLarens of Norris and Oscar Piastri waited until the very end of the session to set their final flying laps.Norris - who was seventh in Q2 then fifth in Q1 - put in a lap of 1m31.824s right at the very end of Q3 as he found a second of laptime between Q2 and Q3.He said it was "probably one of the best laps I've ever done" after taking his third pole position of 2026.Verstappen improved as the clock ran out, but lost time in the final sector to qualify third, behind Antonelli, and 0.140s off Norris's pace.Hamilton lost time in the first sector but still improved, only to qualify fourth and 0.189s off pole.Charles Leclerc was just 0.006s behind Ferrari team-mate Hamilton as he rounded out the top five.Mercedes' George Russell slid out of the final corner on his final effort, losing time and finishing sixth. His pace fell away after a table-topping performance in Q1, as he also finished sixth in Q2.Piastri was off the pace throughout and finished seventh, 0.470s off his polesitting team-mate.The other Red Bull of Liam Lawson was almost half a second off in eighth.Alpine's Franco Colapinto rescued his car after it bottomed out at La Monumental in Q2 as he went on to secure ninth on the grid, having been one second off the pace in Q3.Arvid Lindblad was two tenths further behind as he put his Racing Bulls 10th.In Q2, Verstappen set the pace (with a 1m32.431s) to go 0.160s clear of Antonelli.The speed trap-topping Audis were eliminated in Q2, with Nico Hulkenberg 11th and Gabriel Bortoleto another 0.165s off in 12th.Esteban Ocon was 13th for Haas.Monza polesitter Pierre Gasly lost a laptime to double yellows in Q2 and was eventually eliminated in 14th. "Compared to [FP3] it's a completely different car, I don’t get it," he said over the radio.Replays also showed Gasly tapping the walls on the entry to Turn 16.Racing Bulls's Yuki Tsunoda had a laptime deleted for track limits in Q2 and could not improve sufficiently. He was eliminated in 15th, one place ahead of Williams's Alex Albon - who was 3.101s off the ultimate pace in Q2.Madrilenian Carlos Sainz was eliminated in 17th in Q1, having lapped just 0.005s slower than Williams team-mate Albon - who missed FP3 with suspension damage.Both Aston Martins were eliminated in Q1: Fernando Alonso (18th) missed out by 0.076s and Lance Stroll did not execute a flying lap due to a suspected water pressure issue.Stroll is set to start at the back of the grid with engine penalties.The Cadillacs were split by two seconds with Sergio Perez 19th and Valtteri Bottas 20th.Ollie Bearman failed to turn a lap in Q1 due to his FP3 crash, calling that a "shame" given the potential of his Haas.1 Lando Norris (McLaren) 1m31.824s2 Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) +0.011s3 Max Verstappen (Red Bull) +0.140s4 Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) +0.189s5 Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) +0.195s6 George Russell (Mercedes) +0.325s7 Oscar Piastri (McLaren) +0.470s8 Liam Lawson (Red Bull) +0.492s9 Franco Colapinto (Alpine) +1.079s10 Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls) +1.217s11 Nico Hulkenberg (Audi) +0.019s (to Q3)12 Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi) +0.184s13 Esteban Ocon (Haas) +0.463s14 Pierre Gasly (Alpine) +0.549s15 Yuki Tsunoda (Racing Bulls) +0.880s16 Alex Albon (Williams) +2.328s17 Carlos Sainz (Williams) +0.005s (to Q2)18 Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin) +0.081s19 Sergio Perez (Cadillac) +0.606s20 Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac) +2.704s21 Ollie Bearman (Haas) no time22 Lance Stroll (Aston Martin) no time

item.title: Energy Driven Inflation Complicates Fed Rate Call
item.content:encoded: PNC Chief Investment Officer Amanda Agati is on Bloomberg This Weekend and says the Fed faces a difficult decision as energy-driven inflation pushes markets toward expectations for higher rates, warning that further tightening could risk a policy error. Agati also tells hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini investors are also adjusting to the prospect of a longer Iran war, while strong corporate earnings have pushed concerns about AI spending further into the background. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Number of Vessels Redirected in US Blockade on Iran Reaches 100
item.author: Sam Kim
item.content:encoded: US forces have redirected 100 commercial vessels over the past 60 days since the blockade against Iran resumed, the Central Command says in an update on X.

item.title: Christopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben Delo
item.author: Geraldine McKelvie
item.content:encoded: Party leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’The pledges mean Reform has received a cash injection of £72m in just 24 hours. They are jointly the largest donations made to a UK political party and have intensified calls for restrictions on money received from individual donors.Continue reading...

item.title: Burial of King Oyo takes place in Uganda as news anchor prepares for throne
item.author: Reuters in Kampala
item.content:encoded: Royal guards carry casket through streets of Fort Portal amid row over appointment of Edward Rukidi KijanangomaUganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as ⁠his Tooro kingdom looked to put ⁠a bitter succession battle behind ​it.Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.Continue reading...

item.author: The Race Team

item.title: F1 Spanish GP: Norris snatches last-gasp pole from Antonelli

item.title: A Travers les Hauts de France: Nienke Veenhoven fastest in sprint to claim victory in Écourt-Saint-Quentin
item.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
item.content:encoded: Nienke Veenhoven was the fastest in the late-season one-day race A Travers les Hauts de France, taking the victory in Écourt-Saint-Quentin. The Visma-Lease a Bike rider was the first to cross the line, beating runner-up Shari Bossuyt (AG Insurance-Soudal Team) and third-placed Lara Gillespie (UAE Team L'IMAD).The field tackled 130.5km of racing from Queant to Écourt-Saint-Quentin. Although a flurry of attacks led to several attempts to break away, no decisive move stayed clear. The short-lived moves all came back together for a fast finish sprint into Écourt-Saint-Quentin.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Republican Groups Rush to Paxton’s Aid in Texas After Staying on Sidelines
item.author: Theodore Schleifer
item.content:encoded: An organization allied with Senate G.O.P. leaders has booked more than $51 million in ads. Now, Ken Paxton has a financial edge after months of being outspent by his Democratic rival.

item.title: Iran Nuclear Blind Spot Deepens as IAEA Loses Access
item.content:encoded: Former US Energy Secretary Ernest Moniz says the loss of IAEA access to Iran has created a serious monitoring gap that makes it increasingly difficult to determine the status of the country's nuclear program. Moniz also warns hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini that tight global supplies of diesel and other refined fuels could face additional pressure as US refineries, already running near capacity, approach their fall maintenance season. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Memorial Marco Pantani: Ion Izagirre captures 20th victory of his career from lead group of four
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Ion Izagirre (Cofidis) sprinted to the 20th victory of his career at the Memorial Marco Pantani, the soon-to-retire Basque rider prevailing from a select lead group of four riders in Cesenatico.Izagirre, riding one of the final races of his 16-year pro career, came out on top from a lead group which went clear on the final climb of the day, San Lorenzo in Scanno, 45km from the finish.The quartet of Izagirre, Michael Storer (Tudor), Giulio Pellizzari (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), and Mikkel Honoré (EF Education-EasyPost) built a lead of a minute during the flat run to the line at the end of the 191.6km race.Further back, it was mostly Jayco-AlUla who rode in the chase, hoping to deliver Andrea Vendrame to the line. The efforts behind would cut into the lead, but they wouldn't be enough to bring the move back.Out front, the quartet wouldn't hold their minute lead all the way to the line, but they'd stay away to contest the finish. The attacks up front flew in the final 4km, with Storer going several times.It was back together for the final kilometre, though, despite late moves by Honoré and Pellizzari. In the end, it was Izagirre who had the decisive kick to the line. He beat Pellizzari and Honoré to take the win, while Storer rounded out the top four.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Trump is giving data centers a pass to pollute
item.author: Justine Calma
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump is weakening environmental regulations in the name of speeding up the construction of AI data centers, raising health risks for Americans, a cadre of former EPA officials said this week in a briefing and new report. They are urging - perhaps futilely - the president to adopt a "Data Center Health Protection Pledge" to signal that the administration is taking the environmental threat seriously.

item.title: Taxes wouldn’t fund $5,000 Trump ‘dividend’ if Republicans win midterms, says commerce secretary
item.author: Edward Helmore
item.content:encoded: Lutnick said $500bn of estimated $1tn needed to fund checks to all US adults could come from new visa programDonald Trump’s controversial proposal to give a $5,000 “dividend” to all US adults if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections would not be paid out from US tax revenues, according to the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick.“It’s not tax money,” Lutnick said in an interview with NBC News, adding that the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers”.Continue reading...

item.title: Luxury Shoppers Put Value Ahead of Labels
item.content:encoded: Bloomberg Pursuits Global Luxury Editor editor Chris Rovzar says luxury shoppers are increasingly prioritizing price, quality and lasting value over labels, helping brands such as Coach and Ralph Lauren gain ground as parts of the broader luxury industry struggle. Joining David Gura and Christina Ruffini on Bloomberg This Weekend, Rovzar explains that New York Fashion Week is also showing renewed momentum for American fashion, with heritage brands and designers embracing color, archival influences and more accessible luxury. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Cam Schlittler’s not the AL MVP … right?
item.author: Joshua Diemert
item.content:encoded: Regular readers know that I’ve followed one of the great Cy Young horse races in recent memory, with Cam Schlittler going great start-for-great start with the Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease. We got a little bit of separation this week, as the Athletics touched up Cease for four runs in five innings on Monday, and then Schlittler allowed just a solo shot in seven frames against the Rockies on Tuesday. Cam has crept just ahead by fWAR, enjoys a considerable lead in bWAR, and right now I think would end up at the top of most voters’ ballots.But something struck me in the aftermath of Cam’s night against Colorado, the same night that Aaron Judge returned to the lineup. Cam Schlittler isn’t just the Cy Young favorite, but he’s built himself an MVP case. No pitcher has won the award since Clayton Kershaw for the 2014 Dodgers, and the last AL winner was 2011 Justin Verlander. Yordan Alvarez is in the hunt for the first Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera, Bobby Witt Jr. is probably the best overall player in the league, and if Junior Caminero tops the AL in home runs and plays on the Junior Circuit’s best team, he probably gets his share of votes too.And yet here’s the thing: Cam stacks up fairly against all three of them!Let’s take Yordan, who I think has the inside track on the award right now. Schlittler’s 0.1 fWAR back, a difference that is literally negligible, and more than three-quarters of a win better by bWAR. Alvarez’s candidacy is based around the Triple Crown, probably being the best hitter in baseball, and dragging what we thought was a finally-deflated Houston Astros team to a division title. Crappy AL West or not, that is exactly the blueprint for an MVP, if one for a slightly older voter.Should Alvarez not win the Triple Crown, he loses a bit of his case, though he’s likely still the best hitter in the game on a division winner, one who will have played in the neighborhood of 155 games. That’s the big thing both undercutting Witt’s MVP claim while bolstering his position as best all-around player — the Kansas City shortstop has only played 128 games at time of writing, yet leads the league in fWAR and bWAR among position players. With a solid-but-not-spectacular 18 homers and 124 wRC+, the parts of his game beyond hitting are doing the heavy lifting there as well. All that and the fact that the Royals are so bad work against him when it comes to end of season awards though, and Bobby seems cursed to be the Dave Stieb of shortstops.Junior Caminero, fittingly, is the junior candidate in this slate, trailing the rest of the field pretty clearly by WAR. The home run totals (an AL-leading 39 as of the time of writing) and the Rays’ season of devil magic help fill in some of the gaps that would otherwise leave him a downballot vote-getter that helped a lot of people’s fantasy teams, and in the end he might be just that. Great season, frightening player, but more of a top-five finisher than taking home the hardware.Cam Schlittler leads the entire AL in bWAR, position players or no. He is virtually tied for third in fWAR. Perhaps most key to his case is the way this Yankee team has been beaten up, with four of his fellow starters seeing IL time this year. The Yankees came into the season with more starting pitching than they needed, and it ended up being just enough, with a chunk of that being because Schlittler has been so reliable, not missing a single start. Virtually every member of the regular starting lineup, save Ben Rice and Paul Goldschmidt, has been injured or demoted in some form this year, and the Opening Day center fielder, DH, and second baseman might not even finish the season on the big-league roster.Through all that, the consistent, balancing force has been Cam’s right arm every five days.MVPs are built on a combination of statistical success and compelling narrative — Aaron Judge’s 2022 was at that point his career-best season, but the chase for 62 is what pushed him over the line. Cam has the total value arguments, and certainly if you can make a compelling case for MVP you have to be the favorite for the Cy Young. Moreover, him being at 25 the stabilizing energy for a team that could very well have completely fallen apart, he may end up higher than you think on the ballot that means the most.

item.title: AI Agents Test the Limits of Human Control
item.content:encoded: Future of Life Institute Chair & Co-Founder Max Tegmark joins Bloomberg This Weekend and says recent incidents involving autonomous AI agents show that loss-of-control risks are no longer purely theoretical and warrant stronger safety requirements. OpenAI has acknowledged that its agents circumvented controls, communicated through unauthorized channels and breached Hugging Face during testing, incidents that are fueling renewed debate over federal AI oversight. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Faun Tour Femmes: Juliette Berthet wins three-up sprint to claim stage 3 and take race lead
item.author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
item.content:encoded: Juliette Berthet (FDJ United-SUEZ) was the fastest of a group of three that contested the stage 3 victory at the Faun Tour Femmes. The Frenchwoman took her second stage win in as many days, ahead of rival runner-up Niamh Fisher-Black (Lidl-Trek), while her FDJ United-SUEZ teammate Lauren Dickson finished third in Tournon-sur-Rhône.Berthet's victory launched her into the overall race lead with just one day of racing remaining on Sunday. She now leads the overall classification, tied on time with overnight leader Fisher-Black, and 28 seconds ahead of Dickson.The third stage of the Faun Tour Femmes offered the peloton a 120km race in Tournon-sur-Rhône that included three main climbs: twice over the Côte de Colombier le Vieux and a final climb over Côte de Lemps.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Amodei, Altman, Musk Call for Slowing Development of AI Models
item.author: Kevin Whitelaw and Seth Fiegerman
item.content:encoded: Leaders of the world’s biggest artificial intelligence platforms said it’s time to slow the development pace of their most advanced — and most lucrative — models, citing escalating risks of the technology.

item.title: Higher Interest Rates May Be the New Normal
item.content:encoded: Joining Bloomberg This Weekend, Bloomberg Economics Chief Economist Tom Orlik says higher interest rates may be the new normal, leaving governments, businesses and households facing a mounting cost from debt accumulated during years of cheap borrowing. Orlik tells hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh faces a key test at next week's meeting as markets signal expectations for tighter policy, potentially putting the central bank at odds with President Donald Trump's preference for lower rates. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Six Nigerians extradited to US over $6M online romance scam
item.author: Guardian staff and Associated Press
item.content:encoded: Alleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South AfricaSix Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6m through online romance scams were extradited to the United States on Friday.South African police confirmed they were to be extradited earlier on Friday, while local news in Africa confirmed that the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, known as the Hawks, facilitated their handover to officials from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service at Cape Town international airport, in collaboration with Interpol South Africa.Continue reading...

item.title: Europe’s Solar Boom Has a Storage Problem
item.content:encoded: Solar has become Europe’s largest source of power during summer months, helped by government incentives, falling technology costs and a rapid buildout across rooftops and utility-scale projects. But that success is creating a new problem: on sunny days, Europe can produce more solar power than the system can absorb, pushing wholesale electricity prices to zero or below and leaving some renewable generators suffering from their own success. Industry experts say the answer is not less solar, but more storage, more flexible demand and stronger grids that can move power from where it is generated to where it is needed. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: What it's like watching an F1 crash unfolding in front of you
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: It's the crunch that stands out. That loud, violent, smack of carbonfibre and metal making violent contact with an immovable solid surface is what sticks in your mind when a Formula 1 car crashes into the barriers right in front of you.It is what stands out recalling those moments at the end of the Spanish Grand Prix's FP3 when Ollie Bearman got it all wrong at the Madring's Turn 10 and ended up smashing into the barriers centimetres in front of me.It is what I remember from the other time it happened to me, at the Monaco swimming pool back in 2001, when Ralf Schumacher shunted right at the end of opening practice on Thursday.There is something strange in how your brain processes those moments when the car you are watching is suddenly not doing what you expect it to, and is well off line and travelling in the wrong direction.You see it is going to go all wrong. You see the tyre smoke. You prepare yourself for the impact. Then the contact happens.And then, what must be milliseconds later but seems an eternity: that crunch as the sound catches up with the light. It is that which rams home that this is a big one.After that, the violence dies down, the strewn debris all rolls to a stop, and there is almost a calmness before the marshals get to action.For a driver, these moments must be even harder to process and the emotions more extreme - as afterwards they appear to go through the classic five stages of grief.Observing Bearman, as he sits in the Haas making clear to marshals he is OK, you can sense from the way he holds his head and hands the denial and then anger he has about having binned it right at the end of the final practice session.As he climbs out through a hole in the barriers, there is the depression and then the acceptance of what has happened, as a moped arrives to whisk him away. But he stands there instead, staring into the distance, desperate to watch a crash replay on the big screen behind us.Then, as the adrenaline winds down, Bearman - since ruled out of qualifying - is beckoned to the medical car. He climbs in the back, looking at the badly damaged Haas still wedged up against the wall. There is the acceptance that it is unlikely that this will not hamper the rest of his weekend.As Bearman is driven away, the marshals move into action, lifting the car onto a truck and throwing chunks of wrecked carbonfibre through the gaps in the fence.Drivers had talked before the weekend about the Madring being a punishing venue, and Bearman himself said that the plenty of crashes he had in the sim meant hopefully he had got them out of his system."Like that, you learn exactly where the limits are and you find them in the most efficient way possible," he said. "By doing that, you don't do that on the real track, hopefully…"Unfortunately, real life bites sometimes. And it can be very noisy.
